blocks.text: Moses does not say in exactly what place the bronze serpent was set up; but he relates that the Israelites, setting out from there, encamped in Oboth, Num. XXI, 10. From this it follows that the place was פינון Phinon, or פונון Phunon, of which see Gen. XXXVI, 41. Num. XXXVIII, 42. 43. and 1 Paral. I, 52. For setting out from Phunon they encamped in Oboth, Num. XXXIII, 43. This, moreover, was a place in Idumaea very famous for its copper mines, as is clear from the Fathers, who write Phaeno, Phennen, Fenon and Metallo-fenon; and hence Phaenesia or Phennesia metalla [the Phaenesian or Phennesian mines]. Thus in Eusebius, book 8 of the History, ch. 13, Sylvanus, bishop of the churches around Gaza, and thirty-nine others were beheaded κατὰ τὰ ἐν Φαινοῖ χαλκοῦ μέταλλα [kata ta en Phainoi chalkou metalla], at the copper mines which are in Phaeno. And in Athanasius' Letter To the Solitaries it is related that Eutychius εἰς μέταλλον ἀποσταλῆναι, καὶ μέταλλον οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλ᾽ εἰς τὸ τῆς [eis metallon apostalēnai, kai metallon ouch haplōs, all᾽ eis to tēs] [III, 221] was sent to the mine, and not merely to a mine, but to the mine of Phaeno. And in Epiphanius, on the Meletians: Meletius and many others were driven into exile, ὑπερορισθέντες ἐν τοῖς Φαινήσιος μετάλλοις [hyperoristhentes en tois Phainēsios metallois], banished to the Phaenesian mines. Theodoret, History book 4, ch. 19: Τοῖς Φεννεσίοις καὶ Προκοννησίοις παρεδίδοντο μετάλλοις [Tois Phennesiois kai Prokonnēsiois paredidonto metallois]. They were condemned to the Phennesian and Proconnesian mines. And not much later, of a certain deacon of Damasus: Τοῖς κατὰ Φέννης παρεδόθη μετάλλοις· ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα τοῦ χαλκοῦ· [Tois kata Phennēs paredothē metallois; esti de tauta tou chalkou;] He was condemned to the mines at Phennes, which are copper mines. So also Nicephorus Callistus, book 11, 28. But most explicitly Jerome in the Places: FENON, a camp of the children of Israel in the desert. It was once a city of the Princes of Edom, now a small village in the desert, where copper is dug out of the mines by condemned convicts as their punishment, between the city of Pe- [col. 428] tra and Zoara. Likewise: DEDAN is at the fourth milestone from Metallo-fenon towards the north. To the same I refer these words of Aristeas in the History of the Seventy Translators: Ἐλέγετο δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῶν παρακειμένων ὀρέων τῆς Ἀραβίας μέταλλα χαλκᾶ καὶ σιδηρᾶ συνίστασθαι πρότερον· ἐκλέλειπται δὲ ταῦτα, καθ᾽ ὃν ἐπεκράτησαν χρόνον Πέρσαι [Elegeto de kai ek tōn parakeimenōn oreōn tēs Arabias metalla chalka kai sidēra synistasthai proteron; ekleleiptai de tauta, kath᾽ hon epekratēsan chronon Persai]. It was also said that formerly copper and iron ores were dug from the mountains of Arabia neighbouring (Judaea), but that these had failed (that is, had been neglected, as is clear from what follows) at the time when the Persians held power. From these mines, it seems, was taken the bronze from which the bronze serpent was cast. And perhaps this was not without a mystery. For in this way it could be signified that the body which Christ assumed was not brought from elsewhere, but was born and formed in the very place where he was manifested in the flesh.
